data.content_ref: inline:The target's claim states the preference is defensible 'as a methodological rule to select the theory with the highest empirical content and thus the greatest capacity for future falsification.' But the stated object of defense is 'Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories.' These are distinct criteria. Empirical content is a logical/structural property (what a theory rules out); corroboration is a historical property (having survived severe tests). A theory can have maximal content but zero corroboration (untested), or modest content but high corroboration (well-tested). The non-inductive defense the claim offers — maximizing 'capacity for future falsification' / 'optimal testability' — attaches to content, not to corroboration. The mechanism confirms the conflation, sliding from 'choosing the best-corroborated theory is equivalent to choosing the most severely tested survivor' (historical) to 'selects the theory that currently offers the most precise targets for potential error' (structural). If the real rule is 'select highest content,' then Popper's actual preference for the better-corroborated (past-surviving) theory receives no non-inductive justification from this argument. And the 'pragmatic gamble' framing cannot explain why one would prefer a corroborated theory over an equally contentful but untested one without some expectation that past survival bears on future relevance — which is the very inductive element the claim claims to have expelled.
